Title: AgentPoison: Red-teaming LLM Agents via Poisoning Memory or Knowledge Bases
Abstract: LLM agents have demonstrated remarkable performance across various applications, primarily due to their advanced capabilities in reasoning, utilizing external knowledge and tools, calling APIs, and executing actions to interact with environments. Current agents typically utilize a memory module or a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) mechanism, retrieving past knowledge and instances with similar embeddings from knowledge bases to inform task planning and execution. However, the reliance on unverified knowledge bases raises significant concerns about their safety and trustworthiness. To uncover such vulnerabilities, we propose a novel red teaming approach Agent Poison, the first backdoor attack targeting generic and RAG-based LLM agents by poisoning their long-term memory or RAG knowledge base. In particular, we form the trigger generation process as a constrained optimization to optimize backdoor triggers by mapping the triggered instances to a unique embedding space, so as to ensure that whenever a user instruction contains the optimized backdoor trigger, the malicious demonstrations are retrieved from the poisoned memory or knowledge base with high probability. In the meantime, benign instructions without the trigger will still maintain normal performance. Unlike conventional backdoor attacks, Agent Poison requires no additional model training or fine-tuning, and the optimized backdoor trigger exhibits superior transferability, in-context coherence, and stealthiness. Extensive experiments demonstrate Agent Poison's effectiveness in attacking three types of real-world LLM agents: RAG-based autonomous driving agent, knowledge-intensive QA agent, and healthcare EHRAgent. On each agent, Agent Poison achieves an average attack success rate higher than 80% with minimal impact on benign performance (less than 1%) with a poison rate less than 0.1%.
Major_Contribution_Result: AgentPoison is a training-free backdoor red-teaming attack that poisons an LLM agent's long-term memory or RAG knowledge base so that an optimized trigger causes malicious demonstrations to be retrieved. On three agent settings (RAG autonomous driving, knowledge-intensive QA, and healthcare EHRAgent), the paper reports about 82% retrieval success and 63% end-to-end attack success with under 1% benign-performance drop at a poison rate below 0.1%. The optimized trigger is also shown to transfer across RAG embedders and to resist some perplexity/rephrasing defenses.
Research_Limitations_Challenges: The authors state that while AgentPoison is effective, it requires white-box access to the embedder for trigger optimization. They note transfer across embedders can reduce this barrier when embedders share similar training data distributions, but the white-box optimization assumption remains a core limitation of the attack design.
Critics: This paper is an attack/red-teaming study of memory/RAG poisoning rather than a defense evaluation lifecycle. Reported ASRs are tied to three agent types and constrained optimization with white-box embedder access, so they should not be generalized as universal agent-security failure rates. It does not claim or demonstrate a full mitigation–reassessment pipeline for LLM-agent security evaluation.
